memory_candidates.content: A module-relocation tool cannot distinguish a citation of a CURRENT location (rewrite it) from a HISTORICAL statement about the old one (leave it byte-identical), and architectural decision records consist largely of the latter. Running one over a documented tree silently collapses 'the archive moves from OLD to NEW' into 'moves from NEW to NEW', and a gate-change table's before/after columns into two identical cells -- each individually plausible, so review misses them. It will also rewrite the tool's own worked examples into self-contradictions ('anchored on the full old prefix X, never the bare token X'). Mitigations that work: exclude the tool's own source; hand-audit the diff of every ADR and programme document; and treat a rewrite that makes both sides of a sentence identical as a warning condition rather than a success.

Re-rooting a subtree to a TOP-LEVEL directory silently narrows what path-shaped and module-shaped gates can cover, independently of whether their patterns were widened correctly. A pattern of the form `(A|B|C)/<more>` requires at least one component after the root, and `(A|B)(\.[A-Z]\w*)+` requires at least one dotted suffix; so a citation of the relocated tree's ROOT ITSELF ('OLD/Sub/' -> 'Sub/', 'Old.Sub' -> 'Sub') stops matching entirely, while every citation of a path INSIDE it keeps matching. Measured on one move: 46 gated citations pre-move, 26 post-move, with all 20 losses of exactly this shape. This is not a widening failure and is not repaired by widening; the invariant it leaves uncovered belongs to a directory-existence check instead, which asserts the root's presence and location directly and more strongly than a resolution check would.

When auditing that a rewrite left a class of citations untouched, a before/after COUNT of those citations is confounded whenever the rewrite itself creates new instances of the same shape -- relocating 'FormalSystem/Boneyard' to 'Boneyard' turns every full-prefix citation into a new bare-form one, so the bare-form count rises and proves nothing. The fix is a sentinel pass: re-run the identical rewrite with every replacement swapped for an opaque marker containing none of the tokens being counted, then compare the counts. Preserved instances survive in both; created ones appear in neither. A rule keyed on the bare token would consume pre-existing instances and the two counts diverge, which is exactly the failure the audit exists to catch.
